triage.name: Rhabdomyolysis
triage.reason: Acute presentation with muscle pain, weakness and dark urine after a trigger; classic case with clear labs (CK, myoglobin) and important complications to recognize.
triage.category: muscle injury / acute kidney injury risk

demographics: More common in males, reflecting higher rates of trauma, exertion and substance use
Occurs in athletes, military recruits and people doing unaccustomed strenuous exercise
Seen in patients immobilized after falls, overdose or stroke

risk_factors.text: Unaccustomed strenuous exertion (marathon, military training, CrossFit)
Statins, especially with fibrates or in high dose
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome

family_history: Inherited myopathy or metabolic muscle disease

chief_complaints.text: My urine looks dark, like cola or tea
I feel weak and can't get up
My legs are swollen and sore

hpi.onset: Acute, over hours to a day or two after a trigger such as exertion, trauma, immobilization or drug use
hpi.duration: Hours to several days at presentation
hpi.progression: Muscle pain and weakness worsen over hours; dark urine appears as muscle breakdown continues; swelling and reduced urine output may follow
hpi.location: Diffuse, often worst in the thighs, calves, shoulders and lower back
hpi.quality: Deep, aching and cramping; muscles feel tender and tight
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; pain 6–9/10 and weakness that can make walking or standing difficult

associated_symptoms.text: Urine looks dark, like cola or tea
Passing much less urine than usual
Confusion or feeling out of it

pertinent_negatives: Recent sore throat or upper respiratory infection
Chronic widespread pain for more than three months
Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
argues_against: Chronic widespread pain for more than three months

positives.text: Urine looks dark, like cola or tea
Passing much less urine than usual

argues_against: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants and young children may present with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting and lethargy rather than reporting muscle pain; viral myositis is a common trigger.
May present with falls, immobility, confusion or reduced urine output after a long lie; muscle pain and dark urine are often not reported.
Patients with chronic kidney disease develop acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia earlier and with less muscle breakdown, so dark urine may be absent.
Rhabdomyolysis is rare in pregnancy but can occur with hyperemesis, seizures or trauma; dark urine may be attributed to other causes and the diagnosis delayed.

general.mild: Alert, uncomfortable, able to walk with effort; muscles tender to touch
general.moderate: Ill-appearing, prefers to lie still, grimaces when moving or when muscles are palpated; may need help standing
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, weak, diaphoretic, visibly swollen limbs, reluctant to move; may be confused
general.critical: Lethargic or obtunded, pale, cold, clammy, with marked limb swelling and little spontaneous movement

findings.maneuver: Palpate the large muscle groups of the thighs, calves, shoulders and lower back
Ask the patient to stand from a chair, walk a few steps, or resist hip and shoulder movement
findings.finding: Proximal muscle weakness, worse than pain alone would explain

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the thighs, calves and shoulders for enlargement and tightness
findings.finding: Muscle swelling with a tight, firm feel

findings.maneuver: Palpate the affected limb compartments and passively stretch the fingers or toes
findings.finding: Compartment tenseness with pain on passive stretch, suggesting compartment syndrome

findings.maneuver: Inspect the urine in the collection container or catheter tubing
Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
Palpate the radial pulse or auscultate the heart
Measure blood pressure with the patient supine and after sitting up
findings.finding: Systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg or a drop on standing

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation to person, place and time and attention
Test strength, sensation and reflexes in all four limbs
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory loss or reflex asymmetry

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the small joints of the hands, wrists and knees
findings.finding: No joint swelling, warmth or redness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, including the eyelids, knuckles and extensor surfaces
findings.finding: No rash, heliotrope discoloration or Gottron papules

labs.caveat: The defining lab; values above 5 times the upper limit of normal are used to define clinically significant rhabdomyolysis. CK peaks in 24-72 hours and falls by roughly half each day once the trigger stops.
Potassium leaks from injured muscle; hyperkalemia is the main early cause of death and is worse with acute kidney injury.
Rises early and can rise faster than expected for the degree of dehydration; a low BUN/creatinine ratio favors rhabdomyolysis over prerenal azotemia.
Often rises less than creatinine, giving a low BUN/creatinine ratio.
Released from damaged muscle; hyperphosphatemia with hypocalcemia is characteristic.
Hypocalcemia from calcium depositing in injured muscle; it can later rebound to hypercalcemia during recovery.
Comes from muscle as well as liver; a high AST with a normal or only mildly raised ALT points to muscle injury.
Rises less than AST in muscle injury; a marked rise suggests liver involvement instead.
The dipstick is positive for blood because of myoglobin, but microscopy shows few or no red cells. This mismatch is a key clue.
Few red cells despite a positive blood dipstick, because the pigment is myoglobin rather than intact red cells.
Muddy brown granular casts indicate acute tubular injury from myoglobin.
Low bicarbonate from metabolic acidosis and acute kidney injury.
Prolongs with disseminated intravascular coagulation or liver injury.
Falls with disseminated intravascular coagulation, which can complicate severe rhabdomyolysis.
Acidemia worsens myoglobin kidney injury and increases the risk of arrhythmia from hyperkalemia.
Can rise from myocardial injury in cocaine or stimulant toxicity, or from demand ischemia; interpret with the ECG and symptoms.
Stress hyperglycemia; marked hyperglycemia should prompt consideration of diabetic ketoacidosis as the cause.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging and to guide safe treatment.

findings.finding: ST elevation or depression from myocardial injury in stimulant toxicity

imaging.study: CT of the affected limb without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Concern for compartment syndrome or when the extent of muscle injury is unclear

findings.text: Swollen, hypodense muscle with loss of normal architecture
Muscle edema and stranding of the surrounding fat
Fluid collection or hematoma within the muscle

imaging.study: MRI of the affected limb without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is uncertain or the extent of muscle necrosis needs defining

findings.text: Muscle edema with high T2 signal in the affected compartments

imaging.preferred_when: Bedside assessment of swelling or to look for a fluid collection
Acute kidney injury when obstruction or chronic kidney disease is a concern

findings.text: Normal or increased echogenicity of the kidneys without hydronephrosis
Hydronephrosis suggesting obstruction as an alternative cause
Findings of aspiration or pulmonary edema in the critically ill

initial.why: The key test; a markedly raised CK confirms muscle breakdown and its level tracks severity
Looks for hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, hypocalcemia and acidosis
Blood-positive dipstick with few red cells suggests myoglobin; also looks for casts and other causes
Rules out pregnancy before imaging and guides safe treatment
Detects the peaked T waves and conduction changes of hyperkalemia
Baseline counts and to look for infection or bleeding as a trigger
A high AST with a lower ALT supports muscle rather than liver injury
Hyperphosphatemia supports muscle breakdown and guides calcium management
Hypocalcemia is common and affects monitoring and treatment
Assesses acidosis and oxygenation in moderate to severe cases
initial.only_if: moderate or severe illness, acidosis suspected, or the patient is critically ill

initial.why: Looks for myocardial injury in stimulant toxicity or demand ischemia
initial.only_if: chest pain, stimulant use, or an abnormal ECG

initial.why: Looks for disseminated intravascular coagulation in severe cases

supporting.why: Low magnesium can worsen arrhythmia risk and is corrected with potassium
Rules out obstruction when the cause of acute kidney injury is unclear
supporting.only_if: acute kidney injury with no clear cause or a history of stones

supporting.test: CT of the affected limb without contrast
supporting.why: Defines the extent of muscle injury and looks for a collection
supporting.only_if: marked limb swelling, severe pain, or concern for compartment syndrome

supporting.test: MRI of the affected limb without contrast
supporting.why: Defines the extent of muscle necrosis when the diagnosis is uncertain
supporting.only_if: uncertain diagnosis or need to map the involved muscle

not_indicated.why: Not part of the acute workup; statin use is a trigger but the lipid panel does not change management now
Hypothyroidism is a predisposing factor but thyroid testing does not help the acute diagnosis
Nonspecific and does not distinguish rhabdomyolysis from its look-alikes
Nonspecific; adds nothing to the CK and urinalysis
Not routine; only for respiratory symptoms or suspected aspiration

not_indicated.test: MRI of the affected limb without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for uncertain diagnosis or mapping of involved muscle

decision_points: Check the potassium and ECG early; hyperkalemia is the main early cause of death
Start aggressive IV fluids as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, before the CK result returns
A positive urine blood dipstick with few red cells on microscopy points to myoglobin rather than hematuria
Watch for compartment syndrome in a swollen, tense limb and involve surgery early
Pregnancy test before any imaging in anyone who could be pregnant

criteria.name: Clinical definition of rhabdomyolysis
criteria.summary: A compatible history (trauma, exertion, immobilization, drugs or seizures) with a creatine kinase above five times the upper limit of normal, often with dark urine and a positive urine blood dipstick but few red cells on microscopy.
items: Creatine kinase above five times the upper limit of normal
Dark urine or a positive blood dipstick with few red cells

differential.name: Acute myocardial infarction
differential.why_considered: Chest discomfort, nausea, diaphoresis and a raised troponin can occur in rhabdomyolysis from stimulant toxicity or demand ischemia, and both can present with acute distress.
differential.trigger: Chest pain, pressure or an abnormal ECG in a patient with muscle symptoms

history: Chest pressure or heaviness radiating to the arm or jaw
Shortness of breath and diaphoresis
Known coronary disease or cardiac risk factors
exam: S3 gallop, new murmur or pulmonary crackles
labs: Troponin rising in a typical pattern rather than a single modest elevation
Creatine kinase usually normal or only mildly raised unless there is concurrent muscle injury
ecg: ST elevation or depression in a coronary distribution
New Q waves or reciprocal changes
imaging: Regional wall motion abnormality on echocardiography

differential.name: Acute kidney injury from another cause
differential.why_considered: Reduced urine output, a rising creatinine and dark urine are shared with rhabdomyolysis, and dehydration often coexists.
differential.trigger: Rising creatinine with little or no muscle pain or weakness

history: Recent nephrotoxic drug exposure or contrast
Poor oral intake with vomiting or diarrhea
No trigger of trauma, exertion or immobilization
exam: Signs of volume depletion or overload without muscle tenderness
No limb swelling or compartment tenseness
labs: Creatine kinase normal or only mildly raised
Urine dipstick negative for blood or positive with many red cells rather than myoglobin
BUN/creatinine ratio high in prerenal states
imaging: Renal ultrasound showing hydronephrosis if obstruction is the cause
Small echogenic kidneys suggesting chronic disease

differential.name: Hematuria from urinary tract pathology
differential.why_considered: Dark or bloody urine is a common reason patients present, and a positive urine blood dipstick is seen in both.

history: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Dysuria, frequency or urgency
Passage of clots
labs: Urine microscopy showing many red cells or red cell casts
imaging: Stone or mass on CT urography

differential.name: Inflammatory myositis
differential.why_considered: Muscle pain and weakness with a raised creatine kinase overlap closely with rhabdomyolysis.

history: Weeks to months of progressive proximal weakness
Difficulty rising from a chair or combing hair
No acute trigger such as trauma, exertion or drugs
exam: Symmetrical proximal weakness without marked tenderness
Heliotrope rash or Gottron papules in dermatomyositis
labs: Creatine kinase elevated but usually lower and stable rather than rapidly rising
Positive antinuclear antibody or myositis-specific antibodies
imaging: Muscle edema on MRI in a symmetrical distribution

differential.name: Hypothyroidism-related myopathy
differential.why_considered: Hypothyroidism causes muscle aches, weakness and a mildly raised creatine kinase and is a predisposing factor for rhabdomyolysis.

history: Weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation
Slow onset over months
No acute trigger
exam: Dry skin, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of reflexes
labs: Thyroid-stimulating hormone elevated with low free thyroxine
Creatine kinase mildly raised and stable

differential.name: Fibromyalgia
differential.why_considered: Chronic widespread muscle pain is a common reason patients report myalgia and may be confused with muscle injury.

history: Widespread pain for more than three months
Fatigue and unrefreshing sleep
No acute trigger or dark urine
exam: Diffuse tenderness without swelling or weakness

differential.name: Polymyalgia rheumatica
differential.why_considered: Muscle aching and stiffness in the shoulders and hips can mimic muscle injury, especially in older adults.

history: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Age over 50 with gradual onset
No trigger or dark urine
exam: Pain with movement but preserved strength
labs: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein markedly elevated

differential.name: Viral myositis
differential.why_considered: Viral infection can cause muscle pain, weakness and a raised creatine kinase, particularly in children.

history: Recent upper respiratory infection or viral prodrome
Fever and malaise preceding muscle pain
No trauma, exertion or drug trigger
exam: Diffuse muscle tenderness, often milder than in rhabdomyolysis
labs: Creatine kinase usually lower than in severe rhabdomyolysis
Urine dipstick may be negative for blood
Viral serology or polymerase chain reaction positive when tested

severity.mild: Muscle aches and mild weakness after a clear trigger, creatine kinase 1000-5000 U/L, normal or near-normal kidney function, no dark urine or only trace pigment, and no electrolyte disturbance.
severity.moderate: Marked muscle pain and weakness with dark urine, creatine kinase 5000-20000 U/L, early acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia or hypocalcemia, and tachycardia or mild dehydration.
severity.severe: Creatine kinase 20000-100000 U/L with established acute kidney injury, significant hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, acidosis, hypotension or confusion, and possible compartment syndrome.
severity.critical: Creatine kinase above 100000 U/L with life-threatening hyperkalemia, severe acute kidney injury requiring dialysis, refractory shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation or arrhythmia.

red_flags.finding: Potassium above 6.0 mmol/L or peaked T waves on ECG
red_flags.meaning: Life-threatening hyperkalemia; treat immediately with calcium, insulin and glucose, and consider dialysis

red_flags.finding: Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour or a rapidly rising creatinine
red_flags.meaning: Acute kidney injury from myoglobin; needs aggressive fluids and possibly renal replacement therapy

red_flags.finding: A tense, swollen limb with pain on passive stretch
red_flags.meaning: Compartment syndrome; needs urgent surgical evaluation and possibly fasciotomy
Shock from hypovolemia, sepsis or arrhythmia; needs resuscitation and monitoring
Severe metabolic derangement, cerebral edema or an alternative diagnosis such as neuroleptic malignant syndrome

red_flags.finding: Bleeding, petechiae or a falling fibrinogen
red_flags.meaning: Disseminated intravascular coagulation complicating severe rhabdomyolysis

complications.name: Acute kidney injury
clues: Dark urine with a positive blood dipstick but few red cells
Rising creatinine with a low BUN/creatinine ratio
Muddy brown granular casts on urine microscopy
Reduced urine output

complications.name: Hyperkalemia
clues: Peaked T waves and a widened QRS on ECG
Potassium above 5.5 mmol/L
Muscle weakness or palpitations

complications.name: Compartment syndrome
clues: Tense, swollen limb
Pain on passive stretch of the fingers or toes
Pallor, paresthesia or pulselessness late in the course

complications.name: Metabolic acidosis
clues: Low bicarbonate and low pH on blood gas
Kussmaul respirations in severe cases

complications.name: Hypocalcemia
clues: Calcium below 8.0 mg/dL
Perioral numbness or carpopedal spasm
Prolonged QT interval on ECG

complications.name: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
clues: Bleeding from puncture sites or petechiae
Prolonged PT and aPTT with low fibrinogen
Falling platelets

complications.name: Hypercalcemia during recovery
clues: Calcium rising above normal days into recovery
Nausea, constipation or confusion

complications.name: Chronic kidney disease
clues: Persistently raised creatinine after the acute episode
Proteinuria or reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate on follow-up

special_populations.differences: Infants and young children may present with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting and lethargy rather than reporting muscle pain; viral myositis is a common trigger and the creatine kinase is often lower than in adults.
May present with falls, immobility, confusion or reduced urine output after a long lie; muscle pain and dark urine are often not reported, and acute kidney injury develops earlier.
Patients with chronic kidney disease develop acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia earlier and with less muscle breakdown, so dark urine may be absent and dialysis may be needed sooner.

Rare in pregnancy but can occur with hyperemesis, seizures or trauma; dark urine may be attributed to other causes and the diagnosis delayed, and aggressive fluids are needed to protect both mother and fetus.
Coagulopathy may be worse and the AST and ALT are harder to interpret because both liver and muscle contribute; monitor for bleeding and adjust fluid and electrolyte management.

key_questions.question: What were you doing in the hours to days before this started — any heavy or unaccustomed exercise, trauma, a fall, or a long period lying on the floor?
key_questions.looking_for: A trigger such as crush injury, unaccustomed exertion, prolonged immobilization, seizure or heat exposure

key_questions.question: When did the muscle pain and weakness start, and how fast have they gotten worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute onset over hours to a day or two after a trigger, worsening over hours

key_questions.question: Where do you feel the pain and weakness most — thighs, calves, shoulders, back?
key_questions.looking_for: Diffuse aching and cramping worst in the large proximal and calf muscle groups

key_questions.question: What does your urine look like — has it been dark like cola or tea?
key_questions.looking_for: Tea- or cola-colored urine from myoglobinuria

key_questions.question: How much urine have you been passing, and has it slowed down?
key_questions.looking_for: Reduced urine output suggesting acute kidney injury

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, nausea, vomiting or confusion?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever, nausea and vomiting are common; confusion suggests severe metabolic derangement

key_questions.question: Have you taken any cocaine, amphetamines, heroin or other drugs, or drunk heavily recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Stimulant or opioid use as a trigger, including immobilization after overdose

key_questions.question: Which medications do you take, especially cholesterol-lowering drugs, and have any doses changed recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Statins, especially with fibrates or in high dose, as a trigger

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a seizure, or been told you have a muscle or metabolic disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures, inherited myopathy or metabolic muscle disease as predisposing factors

key_questions.question: Do you have kidney disease, diabetes or thyroid problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic kidney disease, diabetes or hypothyroidism, which lower the threshold for injury and complications

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had muscle disease or problems with anesthesia?
key_questions.looking_for: Inherited myopathy or metabolic muscle disease

key_questions.question: Do your joints hurt or swell, or have you had a rash or a recent sore throat or viral illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; joint pain, rash or a viral prodrome point toward myositis or viral myositis instead

key_questions.question: Have you had any chest pain, shortness of breath or a racing heartbeat?
key_questions.looking_for: Chest pain or palpitations suggesting myocardial injury or hyperkalemic arrhythmia

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes pregnancy before imaging and guides safe treatment

reasoning_points: An acute trigger such as crush injury, unaccustomed exertion, prolonged immobilization, seizure, heat exposure or stimulant or statin use
Diffuse muscle pain, tenderness and weakness with swelling of the large muscle groups
Tea- or cola-colored urine with a positive urine blood dipstick but few red cells on microscopy, indicating myoglobin rather than hematuria
A markedly elevated creatine kinase, above five times the upper limit of normal, confirming muscle breakdown
Supporting labs of hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, a raised AST with a lower ALT, and a low BUN/creatinine ratio
Complications recognized early: acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis and compartment syndrome
Look-alikes excluded, including acute myocardial infarction, other causes of acute kidney injury, hematuria, inflammatory myositis, hypothyroid myopathy, fibromyalgia and polymyalgia rheumatica

easy: Young adult with classic trigger such as a marathon, military training or crush injury
Diffuse muscle pain and weakness with dark cola-colored urine
Markedly elevated creatine kinase with a positive urine blood dipstick and few red cells
Hyperkalemia with peaked T waves on ECG
medium: Older adult found after a long lie with falls, immobility and reduced urine output but no reported muscle pain
Statin plus fibrate use with muscle aches and a modestly raised creatine kinase
Patient with chronic kidney disease who develops acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia with less muscle breakdown
Cocaine or stimulant use with chest discomfort and a raised troponin that must be distinguished from myocardial infarction
hard: Child with irritability, poor feeding and vomiting after a viral illness rather than reported muscle pain
Confused or obtunded patient with no history, where neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome is also possible
Swollen tense limb where compartment syndrome must be recognized and surgery involved early
Severe case with disseminated intravascular coagulation, acidosis and shock where the trigger is unclear
Pregnant patient with dark urine attributed to another cause, delaying the diagnosis
